newsitem.title: JAPAN: Jailed Japanese trader slams US regulators in book.
newsitem.headline: Jailed Japanese trader slams US regulators in book.

text.p: A one-time Daiwa Bank bond trader jailed in a $1.1 billion scandal slams his former employers as well as U.S. and Japanese regulators in a book to go on sale next week.

In "The Confession", Toshihide Iguchi claims investigators at Japan's Finance Ministry and the U.S. Federal Reserve were careless when they failed to detect his wrongdoings in inspections conducted before he eventually confessed to massive unauthorised trading.

He also charges that Daiwa at first attempted to cover up the losses, even filling the trading room where the deals took place with cardboard boxes so regulators would think it was just a storage room.
Daiwa Bank and Finance Ministry spokesmen declined to comment on the book, advance copies of which were made available to reporters on Tuesday.
Iguchi, 45, was sentenced in December to four years in prison for hiding the problem and conspiring with managers to conceal what was one of the biggest financial losses ever.
Iguchi, a Japanese-born bond trader who worked in Daiwa Bank's New York office, pleaded guilty to the unauthorised trading in October 1995.
Daiwa Bank pleaded guilty in February 1996 to 16 charges that it covered up Iguchi's trading losses and agreed to pay a record fine of $340 million.
Daiwa officials have said they learnt of Iguchi's activities when he sent the bank's president a 30-page confession on July 13, 1995.
The bank informed the Finance Ministry in early August, but U.S. officials were not told until six weeks later.
In the book, written in prison, Iguchi said the bank held a secret meeting to discuss how to cover up the loss after receiving his confession.
Daiwa executives who attended the meeting discussed the feasibility of transferring the losses to a paper company in the Cayman Islands, Iguchi wrote.
Iguchi said the New York Fed also failed to detect his misdeeds.
In 1992, Iguchi was trading U.S. securities in a Wall Street office which had not been authorised by the Finance Ministry.
Daiwa stuffed the room with boxes to make it look like a storage space and the Fed's New York examiners were unable to detect the losses, he wrote.
The examination, which was supposed to last two full days, in fact only took 15 minutes, he added.
The Fed knew later in January 1993 about the camouflage, but did not detect Iguchi's unauthorised trading losses.
Daiwa reported the problem to the Finance Ministry in January 1994, but failed to disclose the huge losses involved.
Alarmed by Daiwa's report, the ministry decided to conduct a week-long investigation in New York, which Iguchi said he feared would then uncover the mammoth size of the scandal.
But Iguchi said Japanese investigators spent just one hour at Daiwa's New York midtown branch, chatting with top officials, and did not visit the Wall Street office.
Iguchi said an itinerary showed the investigators next went to Las Vegas.
Despite his prison sentence and lost career, Iguchi said his real friends had remained steadfast.
"All I have lost are things that money can buy. Even strict U.S. prosecutors cannot take away the friendship and love of those people who know my true self," he said in the afterword of the book.

A spokesman for publishing firm Bungei Shunju told a news conference that authors commonly received about 10 percent of sales as royalties for such books and that the initial printing would run to 40,000 copies at 1,500 yen ($13) each. ($1=115 yen)
